svg.title: Bounding a container log in two dimensions, and keeping the end that matters
svg.desc: On the left, a container's whole log is drawn as a tall column running from oldest at the top to newest at the bottom, with two windows nested inside its lower end. The outer window is what tail_lines selects from the API server, which bounds what crosses the wire; the inner window is what max_bytes keeps, which bounds what reaches the model's context window. A note says one line of structured JSON logging can be kilobytes, so a line count is not a size. On the right, two panels of identical geometry compare two ways of cutting that window down, each drawn as the same box with the same dashed rule across its middle. The upper panel, marked with a cross, keeps the oldest end: it is what the API's own limitBytes does when tailLines is set too, reading forward from the start and stopping, and the lines below its rule are the four hundred and seventy newer ones it dropped, including the traceback that explains the crash. The lower panel, marked with a tick, keeps the newest end: the dropped lines sit above the rule and the kept lines below it, a traceback ending in a KeyError, with the cut moved forward to the first newline so no half-line survives. A band across the bottom carries the counters from a real run: truncated true, one thousand nine hundred and seventy-nine bytes returned, thirty-one thousand and twenty bytes and four hundred and seventy lines dropped, measured from a thirty-three kilobyte log read with max_bytes set to two thousand, reported rather than silently discarded.
svg.text: Two bounds, and the end you keep
tail_lines bounds the wire. max_bytes bounds the context. They are not the same bound.
The two bounds act on different things

kilobytes, so a line count is not a size.
